newsitem.title: UK: Drug deaths on increase in British teenagers.
newsitem.headline: Drug deaths on increase in British teenagers.

text.p: More and more British teenagers are trying drugs -- and dying from their effects, researchers reported on Friday.
Ian Roberts and colleagues at London's Institute of Child Health found deaths from accidental overdoses and side-effects had increased by eight percent each year between 1985 to 1995.
"There has been a large increase in the death rates from accidental poisoning among teenagers aged 15 to 19 years," they wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal.
"The increase is particularly noticeable for opiates and related narcotics and for psychostimulant drugs (such as Ecstasy or MDMA)."
Roberts's group looked at all records for deaths from injury and poisoning in England and Wales for teenagers.
"Over the 11 years 436 teenagers died of accidental poisoning; 303 were males and 133 females," they wrote.
"The largest single category of death from poisoning was accidental poisoning by opiates and related narcotics, which accounted for 21 percent of the deaths."

They referred to other studies that showed the number of teenagers being offered drugs had skyrocketed. One found the percentage of schoolchildren who had been offered Ecstasy had gone from five percent to 43 percent between 1989 and 1994.
There have been several high-profile cases of teenagers dying from a single dose of Ecstasy in Britain. Opiates such as heroin are also dangerously toxic.
